agents execute repo or ledger changes and reply. | primary | A.4 |\n/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.decision-os/cards/tasks-system/card-codex-skill-1783427295206-134c02c5.md:26:| F14 | `workflow` | CLI workflows support maintenance, agent queue handling, generator work, and ledger treatment outside the browser. | supporting | A.2, C.1, C.4 |\n/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.decision-os/cards/tasks-system/card-codex-skill-1783427295206-134c02c5.md:27:| F15 | `use_constraint` | Product boundaries remain open for reports, watcher loops, work queues, and goal-object UX. | primary | A.6, A.7, D.5 |\n/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.decision-os/cards/tasks-system/card-codex-skill-1783427295206-134c02c5.md:33:- **Decision workspace:** `decision-os` turns local ledger files into a browser canvas for specs, data, performance evidence, and task planning.\n/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.decision-os/cards/tasks-system/card-codex-skill-1783427295206-134c02c5.md:35:- **Agent handoff:** agents read operator notes, change repo or ledger state, and answer in durable `# AGENT` sections.\n/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.decision-os/c…18782 tokens truncated…re not available elsewhere (Ross et al 2009, Jones et al 2015, Baudard et al 2017).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:14:    <block index=\"9\" kind=\"paragraph\">Clinical study reports (CSRs) contain unabridged and comprehensive descriptions of the clinical problem, design, conduct and results of clinical trials, following a structure and content guidance prescribed by the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH 1995). To obtain marketing approval of drugs and biologics for a specific indication, pharmaceutical companies submit CSRs and other required materials to regulatory authorities. Because CSRs also incorporate tables and figures, with appendices containing the protocol, statistical analysis plan, sample case report forms, and patient data listings (including narratives of all serious adverse events), they can be thousands of pages in length. CSRs often contain more data about trial methods and results than any other single data source (Mayo-Wilson et al 2018). CSRs are often difficult to access, and are usually not publicly available. Review authors could request CSRs from the European Medicines Agency (Davis and Miller 2017). The US Food and Drug and Administration had historically avoided releasing CSRs but launched a pilot programme in 2018 whereby selected portions of CSRs for new drug applications were posted on the agency’s website. Many CSRs are obtained through unsealed litigation documents, repositories (e.g. clinicalstudydatarequest.com), and other open data and data-sharing channels (e.g. The Yale University Open Data Access Project) (Doshi et al 2013, Wieland et al 2014, Mayo-Wilson et al 2018)).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:36:    <block index=\"31\" kind=\"paragraph\">date and duration of the study (which also can clarify whether different sample sizes are due to different periods of recruitment), length of follow-up, or subgroups selected to address secondary goals.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:94:    <block index=\"89\" kind=\"paragraph\">For the purposes of this chapter, we define ‘data’ to be any information about (or derived from) a study, including details of methods, participants, setting, context, interventions, outcomes, results, publications, and investigators. Review authors should plan in advance what data will be required for their systematic review, and develop a strategy for obtaining them (see MECIR Box 5.3.a). The involvement of consumers and other stakeholders can be helpful in ensuring that the categories of data collected are sufficiently aligned with the needs of review users (Chapter 1, Section 1.3). The data to be sought should be described in the protocol, with consideration wherever possible of the issues raised in the rest of this chapter.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:129:    <block index=\"124\" kind=\"paragraph\">Integrity of interventions (i.e. the degree to which specified procedures or components of the intervention were implemented as planned)</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:146:    <block index=\"141\" kind=\"paragraph\">If subgroup analysis is planned, the same information would need to be extracted for each participant subgroup</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:173:    <block index=\"168\" kind=\"paragraph\">any strategies used to ensure or assess fidelity or adherence to the intervention, and the extent to which the intervention was delivered as planned.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:177:    <block index=\"172\" kind=\"paragraph\">The degree to which specified procedures or components of the intervention are implemented as planned can have important consequences for the findings from a study. We describe this as intervention integrity; related terms include adherence, compliance and fidelity (Carroll et al 2007). The verification of intervention integrity may be particularly important in reviews of non-pharmacological trials such as behavioural interventions and complex interventions, which are often implemented in conditions that present numerous obstacles to idealized delivery.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:178:    <block index=\"173\" kind=\"paragraph\">It is generally expected that reports of randomized trials provide detailed accounts of intervention implementation (Zwarenstein et al 2008, Moher et al 2010). In assessing whether interventions were implemented as planned, review authors should bear in mind that some interventions are standardized (with no deviations permitted in the intervention protocol), whereas others explicitly allow a degree of tailoring (Zwarenstein et al 2008). In addition, the growing field of implementation science has led to an increased awareness of the impact of setting and context on delivery of interventions (Damschroder et al 2009). (See Chapter 17, Section 17.1.2.1 for further information and discussion about how an intervention may be tailored to local conditions in order to preserve its integrity.)</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:185:    <block index=\"180\" kind=\"paragraph\">An outcome is an event or a measurement value observed or recorded for a particular person or intervention unit in a study during or following an intervention, and that is used to assess the efficacy and safety of the studied intervention (Meinert 2012). Review authors should indicate in advance whether they plan to collect information about all outcomes measured in a study or only those outcomes of (pre-specified) interest in the review. Research has shown that trials addressing the same condition and intervention seldom agree on which outcomes are the most important, and consequently report on numerous different outcomes (Dwan et al 2014, Ismail et al 2014, Denniston et al 2015, Saldanha et al 2017a). The selection of outcomes across systematic reviews of the same condition is also inconsistent (Page et al 2014, Saldanha et al 2014, Saldanha et al 2016, Liu et al 2017). Outcomes used in trials and in systematic reviews of the same condition have limited overlap (Saldanha et al 2017a, Saldanha et al 2017b).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:215:    <block index=\"210\" kind=\"paragraph\">Reports of studies often include several results for the same outcome. For example, different measurement scales might be used, results may be presented separately for different subgroups, and outcomes may have been measured at different follow-up time points. Variation in the results can be very large, depending on which data are selected (Gøtzsche et al 2007, Mayo-Wilson et al 2017a). Review protocols should be as specific as possible about which outcome domains, measurement tools, time points, and summary statistics (e.g. final values versus change from baseline) are to be collected (Mayo-Wilson et al 2017b). A framework should be pre-specified in the protocol to facilitate making choices between multiple eligible measures or results. For example, a hierarchy of preferred measures might be created, or plans articulated to select the result with the median effect size, or to average across all eligible results for a particular outcome domain (see also Chapter 9, Section 9.3.3). Any additional decisions or changes to this framework made once the data are collected should be reported in the review as changes to the protocol.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:226:    <block index=\"221\" kind=\"paragraph\">We recommend that review authors collect the key conclusions of the included study as reported by its authors. It is not necessary to report these conclusions in the review, but they should be used to verify the results of analyses undertaken by the review authors, particularly in relation to the direction of effect. Further comments by the study authors, for example any explanations they provide for unexpected findings, may be noted. References to other studies that are cited in the study report may be useful, although review authors should be aware of the possibility of citation bias (see Chapter 7, Section 7.2.3.2). Documentation of any correspondence with the study authors is important for review transparency.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:266:    <block index=\"261\" kind=\"item\">Can record notes and explanations easily</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:345:    <block index=\"340\" kind=\"paragraph\">CSRs may contain many outcomes and present many results for a single outcome (due to different analyses) (Mayo-Wilson et al 2017b). We recommend review authors extract results only for outcomes of interest to the review (Section 5.3.6). With regard to different methods of analysis, review authors should have a plan and pre-specify preferred metrics in their protocol for extracting results pertaining to different populations (e.g. ‘all randomized’, ‘all participants taking at least one dose of medication’), methods for handling missing data (e.g. ‘complete case analysis’, ‘multiple imputation’), and adjustment (e.g. unadjusted, adjusted for baseline covariates). It may be important to record the range of analysis options available, even if not all are extracted in detail. In some cases it may be preferable to use metrics that are comparable across multiple included studies, which may not be clear until data collection for all studies is complete.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:352:    <block index=\"347\" kind=\"paragraph\">Sometimes numerical data needed for systematic reviews are only presented in figures. Review authors may request the data from the study investigators, or alternatively, extract the data from the figures either manually (e.g. with a ruler) or by using software. Numerous tools are available, many of which are free. Those available at the time of writing include tools called Plot Digitizer, WebPlotDigitizer, Engauge, Dexter, ycasd, GetData Graph Digitizer. The software works by taking an image of a figure and then digitizing the data points off the figure using the axes and scales set by the users. The numbers exported can be used for systematic reviews, although additional calculations may be needed to obtain the summary statistics, such as calculation of means and standard deviations from individual-level data points (or conversion of time-to-event data presented on Kaplan-Meier plots to hazard ratios; see Chapter 6, Section 6.8.2).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:366:    <block index=\"361\" kind=\"heading\">5.5.11 Key points in planning and reporting data extraction</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:419:    <block index=\"414\" kind=\"paragraph\">Liberati A, Altman DG, Tetzlaff J, Mulrow C, Gøtzsche PC, Ioannidis JPA, Clarke M, Devereaux PJ, Kleijnen J, Moher D. The PRISMA statement for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies that evaluate health care interventions: explanation and elaboration. PLoS Medicine 2009; 6: e1000100.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/cochrane-data-collection.xml:430:    <block index=\"425\" kind=\"paragraph\">Moher D, Hopewell S, Schulz KF, Montori V, Gøtzsche PC, Devereaux PJ, Elbourne D, Egger M, Altman DG. CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ 2010; 340: c869.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:268:    <block index=\"263\" kind=\"item\">This section introduces provenance concepts with informal explanations and illustrative</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:453:    <block index=\"448\" kind=\"paragraph\">in Section 5.3.3). Agents may rely on plans, i.e. sets of actions or steps, to achieve their</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:454:    <block index=\"449\" kind=\"paragraph\">goals in the context of an activity.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:456:    <block index=\"451\" kind=\"paragraph\">association relation allows for a plan to be specified. Plan is defined by subtyping and</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:458:    <block index=\"453\" kind=\"paragraph\">A plan is an entity that represents a set of actions or steps intended by one or more agents to achieve some goals.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:459:    <block index=\"454\" kind=\"paragraph\">An activity association is an assignment of responsibility to an agent for an activity, indicating that the agent had a role in the activity. It further allows for a plan to be specified, which is the plan intended by the agent to achieve some goals in the context of this activity.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:461:    <block index=\"456\" kind=\"paragraph\">prescriptive requirements on the nature of plans, their representation, the</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:462:    <block index=\"457\" kind=\"paragraph\">actions or steps they consist of, or their intended goals. Since plans may evolve over time,</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:463:    <block index=\"458\" kind=\"paragraph\">it may become necessary to track their provenance, so plans themselves are</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:464:    <block index=\"459\" kind=\"paragraph\">entities. Representing the plan explicitly in the provenance can be useful for various tasks: for example, to</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:466:    <block index=\"461\" kind=\"paragraph\">manage expectation failures, or to provide explanations.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:468:    <block index=\"463\" kind=\"paragraph\">An example of association between an activity and an agent involving a plan is:</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:469:    <block index=\"464\" kind=\"paragraph\">an XSLT transform (an activity) launched by a user (an agent) based on an XSL style sheet (a plan).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:588:    <block index=\"583\" kind=\"paragraph\">Agents were assigned various responsibilities in the editing activity: contributor and editor. The plan the agent relied upon is not specified, hence, the marker '-'.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:614:    <block index=\"609\" kind=\"paragraph\">Documents were published according to the process rules (process:rec-advance), a plan in PROV terminology.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:629:    <block index=\"624\" kind=\"paragraph\">This relation is illustrated in Figure 3 with a multi-edge labelled wasAssociatedWith pointing to an agent and entity (representing a plan).</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:630:    <block index=\"625\" kind=\"paragraph\">This simple example has shown a variety of PROV concepts, such as Entity, Agent, Activity, Usage, Generation, Derivation, and Association. In this example, it happens that all entities were already Web resources, with readily available IRIs, which we used. We note that some of the resources are public, whereas others have restricted access: provenance statements only make use of their identifiers. If identifiers do not pre-exist, e.g. for activities, then they can be generated, for instance ex:act2, occurring in the namespace identified by prefix ex. We note that the IRI scheme developed by W3C is particularly suited for expressing provenance of these documents, since each IRI denotes a specific version of a document. It then becomes easy to relate the various versions with PROV relations. We note that an Association is a ternary relation (represented by a multi-edge labeled wasAssociatedWith) from an activity to an agent and a plan.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:710:    <block index=\"705\" kind=\"item\">WasAssociatedWith (plan)</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:951:    <block index=\"946\" kind=\"paragraph\">The Painter, a Picasso painting, is known to have been destroyed in a plane accident.</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:956:    <block index=\"951\" kind=\"paragraph\">wasInvalidatedBy(ex:The-Painter, ex:crash, 1998-09-03T01:31:00, [ ex:circumstances=\"plane accident\" ])</block>\n/home/jbb/.codex/skills/corpus-data-extraction/references/w3c-prov-data-model.xml:1135:    <block index=\"1130\" kind=\"paragraph\">An activity association ◊ is an assignment of responsibility to an agent for an activity, indicating that the agent had a role in the activity. They are not the right place to own scheduling, leases, long-running progress, blocking state, approval gates, dependency order, or multi-agent coordination.\n\nThe better model is:\n\n1. **Threads:** conversation history.\n2. **Tasks:** durable units of work created from operator intent.\n3. **Runs:** execution attempts on those tasks.\n\nThis gives the operator a multi-thread decision process without forcing every agent to infer state from the latest note in every thread.\n\n---\n\n## Current Constraint\n\nThe current system can already find unanswered threads and append agent answers:\n\n- `ledger-cli unanswered` scans thread notes where operator notes appear after the last agent answer.\n- `ledger-cli answer` appends a single agent reply.\n- Card processing status currently infers work from thread note ownership.\n\nThat is useful, but it overloads threads as:\n\n- a queue\n- a lock\n- a status model\n- a transcript\n- a progress log\n- a recovery surface\n\nThose are different responsibilities and they should not live in one structure.\n\n---\n\n## Recommended Direction\n\nAdd a workspace-local work queue:\n\n```text\n.decision-os/\n  agent-runs/\n    tasks.json\n    runs/\n      run-<timestamp>-<id>.json\n    logs/\n      run-<timestamp>-<id>.md\n```\n\nThe operator can still write naturally in card, zone, group, or canvas threads. A task extractor turns eligible operator notes into tasks. Agents work from the task queue, not from raw unanswered-thread scans.\n\n---\n\n## Task Shape\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"task-20260706-001\",\n  \"createdAt\": \"2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z\",\n  \"updatedAt\": \"2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z\",\n  \"status\": \"ready\",\n  \"priority\": 50,\n  \"source\": {\n    \"ledgerFile\": \".decision-os/next-features.json\",\n    \"threadId\": \"thread-card-...\",\n    \"noteId\": \"note-operator-...\",\n    \"targetKind\": \"card\",\n    \"targetId\": \"card-...\"\n  },\n  \"title\": \"Short work title\",\n  \"request\": \"Operator-authored request or extracted summary.\",\n  \"scope\": {\n    \"workspaceRoot\": \"/path/to/workspace\",\n    \"allowedPaths\": [],\n    \"ledgerFiles\": [\".decision-os/next-features.json\"]\n  },\n  \"dependencies\": [],\n  \"approval\": {\n    \"required\": false,\n    \"reason\": \"\"\n  },\n  \"lease\": null,\n  \"lastRunId\": null\n}\n```\n\nTask statuses:\n\n- `triage`: captured but not yet ready.\n- `ready`: available to claim.\n- `leased`: claimed with a lease expiry.\n- `running`: actively executing.\n- `waiting-operator`: paused on an explicit decision request.\n- `blocked`: cannot proceed without external state or missing information.\n- `verifying`: implementation is done and checks are running.\n- `done`: completed and reported.\n- `cancelled`: intentionally stopped.\n\n---\n\n## Run Shape\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"run-20260706-001\",\n  \"taskId\": \"task-20260706-001\",\n  \"agentId\": \"codex-<host>-<pid>\",\n  \"startedAt\": \"2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z\",\n  \"updatedAt\": \"2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z\",\n  \"status\": \"running\",\n  \"leaseExpiresAt\": \"2026-07-06T00:20:00.000Z\",\n  \"phase\": \"implementation\",\n  \"progress\": [\n    {\n      \"at\": \"2026-07-06T00:00:00.000Z\",\n      \"kind\": \"observation\",\n      \"message\": \"Located relevant files and tests.\"\n    }\n  ],\n  \"outputs\": {\n    \"changedFiles\": [],\n    \"tests\": []\n  }\n}\n```\n\nRun statuses:\n\n- `running`\n- `renewed`\n- `waiting-operator`\n- `failed`\n- `completed`\n- `abandoned`\n\n---\n\n## Scheduling Rules\n\n1. A worker claims one task by atomically setting `status=leased`, `lease.agentId`, and `lease.expiresAt`.\n2. A task with an expired lease returns to `ready` unless the active run is waiting for the operator.\n3. Agents renew leases while doing long work.\n4. An agent may process multiple tasks only when they are independent and in the same workspace.\n5. Dependencies are task ids. A task is runnable only when all dependencies are `done`.\n6. Destructive actions, pushes, broad refactors, and ambiguous scope changes require an approval gate unless the operator already authorized them.\n\n---\n\n## Operator Interaction\n\nWhen an operator note implies work, decision-os creates or updates a linked task and can add a small marker to the thread:\n\n```markdown\n# SYSTEM\n<!-- decision-os:task {\"id\":\"task-20260706-001\",\"status\":\"ready\"} -->\nTask queued for autonomous work.\n```\n\nWhen an agent needs a decision, it writes both:\n\n- `task.status = waiting-operator`\n- a normal `# AGENT` note in the source thread with the exact question\n\nWhen work completes, it writes:\n\n- `task.status = done`\n- run evidence with changed files and checks\n- a concise `# AGENT` answer in the source thread\n\nThis keeps threads readable while making execution state inspectable.\n\n---\n\n## CLI Surface\n\nStart with CLI commands before deeper UI integration:\n\n```bash\nledger-cli tasks list --root /path/to/workspace\nledger-cli tasks extract --ledger .decision-os/next-features.json\nledger-cli tasks claim --root /path/to/workspace --agent-id codex-a --json\nledger-cli tasks renew --task-id task-... --run-id run-...\nledger-cli tasks progress --task-id task-... --run-id run-... --message \"...\"\nledger-cli tasks wait-operator --task-id task-... --message-file question.md\nledger-cli tasks complete --task-id task-... --run-id run-... --summary-file summary.md\nledger-cli tasks release --task-id task-...\n```\n\nFirst useful implementation:\n\n1. `tasks extract`\n2. `tasks list`\n3. `tasks claim`\n4. `tasks complete`\n\nThis replaces manual unanswered-thread polling with a durable queue while keeping the old command available.\n\n---\n\n## UI Surface\n\nShort term:\n\n- Card badge uses linked task status before falling back to note-role inference.\n- Thread panel shows linked task id and status near the target title.\n- A workspace-level Agent Work drawer lists ready, running, blocked, and waiting tasks.\n\nMedium term:\n\n- Canvas zones can group task batches.\n- Operators can approve, cancel, reprioritize, or split tasks.\n- Long-running runs stream progress into the drawer without adding noisy notes to the thread.\n\n---\n\n## Autonomy Contract\n\nAn autonomous agent loop should:\n\n1. Load workspace instructions and task queue.\n2. Claim the highest-priority runnable task.\n3. Read the source thread, target card or zone, linked ledgers, and relevant files.\n4. Write a run checkpoint before editing.\n5. Implement the smallest structurally correct change.\n6. Verify with targeted tests or explicit manual checks.\n7. Renew the lease as needed.\n8. Ask the operator only when the task is ambiguous, high-risk, or externally blocked.\n9. Complete the task with evidence and answer the source thread.\n10. Claim the next runnable task if budget remains.\n\nThis increases autonomy without removing operator control.\n\n---\n\n## Failure Recovery\n\n- Expired leases are visible and reclaimable.\n- Runs are not deleted by default.\n- A resumed agent reads the latest run log before continuing.\n- A failed run records the blocking condition and suggested next action.\n- If a task fails repeatedly, it moves to `blocked` instead of looping.\n\n---\n\n## Implementation Phases\n\n### Phase 1: Queue Core\n\n- Add task/run types to `ledger-cli`.\n- Add helpers to read/write `.decision-os/agent-runs/tasks.json`.\n- Add `tasks extract`, `tasks list`, `tasks claim`, and `tasks complete`.\n- Keep extraction conservative: one ready task per unanswered thread.\n- Add unit tests for status transitions and lease expiry.\n\n### Phase 2: Status Integration\n\n- Update card work status resolution to check linked tasks.\n- Add a backend route to expose task summary with the active ledger payload.\n- Show task status in card chrome and thread header.\n- Preserve current note-role fallback for old workspaces.\n\n### Phase 3: Operator Control\n\n- Add a workspace Agent Work drawer.\n- Add approve, cancel, reprioritize, and release actions.\n- Add `waiting-operator` rendering with direct thread focus.\n\n### Phase 4: Long-Run Execution\n\n- Add a runner command that loops over `claim -> work -> complete`.\n- Add lease renewal and progress append commands.\n- Add stale run recovery.\n- Add per-task autonomy budgets and approval policies.\n\n---\n\n## First Cut\n\nBuild Phase 1 first and do not modify the frontend yet.\n\nThe highest-yield change is a durable queue that can be driven by CLI and inspected in git. Once the queue proves useful, the frontend should render it. Starting with UI would preserve the core flaw: visible threads would still be carrying execution state they cannot safely own.\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3d8c-b368-7a22-91d2-384091eef0b2"}}}

Use when the user wants to validate that implementation is complete, correct, and coherent before archiving.\nlicense: MIT\ncompatibility: Requires openspec CLI.\nmetadata:\n  author: openspec\n  version: \"1.0\"\n  generatedBy: \"1.0.2\"\n---\n\nVerify that an implementation matches the change artifacts (specs, tasks, design).\n\n**Input**: Optionally specify a change name. If omitted, check if it can be inferred from conversation context. If vague or ambiguous you MUST prompt for available changes.\n\n**Steps**\n\n1. **If no change name provided, prompt for selection**\n\n   Run `openspec list --json` to get available changes. Use the **AskUserQuestion tool** to let the user select.\n\n   Show changes that have implementation tasks (tasks artifact exists).\n   Include the schema used for each change if available.\n   Mark changes with incomplete tasks as \"(In Progress)\".\n\n   **IMPORTANT**: Do NOT guess or auto-select a change. Always let the user choose.\n\n2. **Check status to understand the schema**\n   ```bash\n   openspec status --change \"<name>\" --json\n   ```\n   Parse the JSON to understand:\n   - `schemaName`: The workflow being used (e.g., \"spec-driven\")\n   - Which artifacts exist for this change\n\n3. **Get the change directory and load artifacts**\n\n   ```bash\n   openspec instructions apply --change \"<name>\" --json\n   ```\n\n   This returns the change directory and context files. Read all available artifacts from `contextFiles`.\n\n4. **Initialize verification report structure**\n\n   Create a report structure with three dimensions:\n   - **Completeness**: Track tasks and spec coverage\n   - **Correctness**: Track requirement implementation and scenario coverage\n   - **Coherence**: Track design adherence and pattern consistency\n\n   Each dimension can have CRITICAL, WARNING, or SUGGESTION issues.\n\n5. **Verify Completeness**\n\n   **Task Completion**:\n   - If tasks.md exists in contextFiles, read it\n   - Parse checkboxes: `- [ ]` (incomplete) vs `- [x]` (complete)\n   - Count complete vs total tasks\n   - If incomplete tasks exist:\n     - Add CRITICAL issue for each incomplete task\n     - Recommendation: \"Complete task: <description>\" or \"Mark as done if already implemented\"\n\n   **Spec Coverage**:\n   - If delta specs exist in `openspec/changes/<name>/specs/`:\n     - Extract all requirements (marked with \"### Requirement:\")\n     - For each requirement:\n       - Search codebase for keywords related to the requirement\n       - Assess if implementation likely exists\n     - If requirements appear unimplemented:\n       - Add CRITICAL issue: \"Requirement not found: <requirement name>\"\n       - Recommendation: \"Implement requirement X: <description>\"\n\n6. **Verify Correctness**\n\n   **Requirement Implementation Mapping**:\n   - For each requirement from delta specs:\n     - Search codebase for implementation evidence\n     - If found, note file paths and line ranges\n     - Assess if implementation matches requirement intent\n     - If divergence detected:\n       - Add WARNING: \"Implementation may diverge from spec: <details>\"\n       - Recommendation: \"Review <file>:<lines> against requirement X\"\n\n   **Scenario Coverage**:\n   - For each scenario in delta specs (marked with \"#### Scenario:\"):\n     - Check if conditions are handled in code\n     - Check if tests exist covering the scenario\n     - If scenario appears uncovered:\n       - Add WARNING: \"Scenario not covered: <scenario name>\"\n       - Recommendation: \"Add test or implementation for scenario: <description>\"\n\n7. **Verify Coherence**\n\n   **Design Adherence**:\n   - If design.md exists in contextFiles:\n     - Extract key decisions (look for sections like \"Decision:\", \"Approach:\", \"Architecture:\")\n     - Verify implementation follows those decisions\n     - If contradiction detected:\n       - Add WARNING: \"Design decision not followed: <decision>\"\n       - Recommendation: \"Update implementation or revise design.md to match reality\"\n   - If no design.md: Skip design adherence check, note \"No design.md to verify against\"\n\n   **Code Pattern Consistency**:\n   - Review new code for consistency with project patterns\n   - Check file naming, directory structure, coding style\n   - If significant deviations found:\n     - Add SUGGESTION: \"Code pattern deviation: <details>\"\n     - Recommendation: \"Consider following project pattern: <example>\"\n\n8. **Generate Verification Report**\n\n   **Summary Scorecard**:\n   ```\n   ## Verification Report: <change-name>\n\n   ### Summary\n   | Dimension    | Status           |\n   |--------------|------------------|\n   | Completeness | X/Y tasks, N reqs|\n   | Correctness  | M/N reqs covered |\n   | Coherence    | Followed/Issues  |\n   ```\n\n   **Issues by Priority**:\n\n   1. **CRITICAL** (Must fix before archive):\n      - Incomplete tasks\n      - Missing requirement implementations\n      - Each with specific, actionable recommendation\n\n   2. **WARNING** (Should fix):\n      - Spec/design divergences\n      - Missing scenario coverage\n      - Each with specific recommendation\n\n   3. **SUGGESTION** (Nice to fix):\n      - Pattern inconsistencies\n      - Minor improvements\n      - Each with specific recommendation\n\n   **Final Assessment**:\n   - If CRITICAL issues: \"X critical issue(s) found. Fix before archiving.\"\n   - If only warnings: \"No critical issues. Y warning(s) to consider. Ready for archive (with noted improvements).\"\n   - If all clear: \"All checks passed. Ready for archive.\"\n\n**Verification Heuristics**\n\n- **Completeness**: Focus on objective checklist items (checkboxes, requirements list)\n- **Correctness**: Use keyword search, file path analysis, reasonable inference - don't require perfect certainty\n- **Coherence**: Look for glaring inconsistencies, don't nitpick style\n- **False Positives**: When uncertain, prefer SUGGESTION over WARNING, WARNING over CRITICAL\n- **Actionability**: Every issue must have a specific recommendation with file/line references where applicable\n\n**Graceful Degradation**\n\n- If only tasks.md exists: verify task completion only, skip spec/design checks\n- If tasks + specs exist: verify completeness and correctness, skip design\n- If full artifacts: verify all three dimensions\n- Always note which checks were skipped and why\n\n**Output Format**\n\nUse clear markdown with:\n- Table for summary scorecard\n- Grouped lists for issues (CRITICAL/WARNING/SUGGESTION)\n- Code references in format: `file.ts:123`\n- Specific, actionable recommendations\n- No vague suggestions like \"consider reviewing\"\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3da1-f52c-7c52-a8bd-de5a1efc1d7f"}}}

Overview & Mental Model\n\n**Singleton factory loop** — one instance, one repo at a time, runs forever. Not a droid — a global background service visible from any droid's scripts overlay.\n\n```\nDroidMaster Backend                        DroidFactory (standalone)\n┌──────────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────────┐\n│  FactoryLoopService  │──spawns/imports──▶  runStep(config)    │\n│  (singleton)         │◀──StepSummary────│  (async generator)  │\n│                      │                 │                      │\n│  REST: /factory/*    │                 │  CLI preserved:      │\n│  Events: factory.*   │                 │  factory-loop.ts     │\n└──────────────────────┘                 └──────────────────────┘\n        │\n        ▼ broadcasts via existing WS\n┌──────────────────────┐\n│  Flutter UI           │\n│  - Factory loop row   │\n│  - Issue pipeline cards│\n│  - Action buttons     │\n└──────────────────────┘\n```\n\n**Key invariants:**\n\n- DroidFactory stays standalone — DroidMaster integration is additive\n- Loop state persisted to `.state/factory-loop.json`, survives restarts\n- One repo at a time — switchable between iterations (not mid-step)\n- Factory events are global (broadcast to all droid WS subscribers)\n\n---\n\n## 2. DroidFactory Changes\n\n### 2.1 Engine Extraction (`src/runner/engine.ts`)\n\nCurrently `src/runner/index.ts` exports a monolithic `main()` that returns `Promise<StepSummary>`:\n\n```typescript\n// Current signature (src/runner/index.ts:204)\nasync function main(): Promise<StepSummary>\n\n// Current StepSummary (src/runner/index.ts:50-60)\ninterface StepSummary {\n  ok: boolean;\n  reason: StepReason;   // 'processed' | 'idle' | 'agent_running' | 'dry_run_actionable' | 'dry_run_idle' | 'config_error' | 'error'\n  exitCode: number;\n  projectUri?: string;\n  processedIssueIid?: number;\n  actionableIssues?: number;\n  scannedIssues?: number;\n  startedAt: string;\n  finishedAt: string;\n}\n```\n\n**Refactor** into an importable engine:\n\n```typescript\n// NEW: src/runner/engine.ts\n\nexport interface StepConfig {\n  projectRoot: string;\n  gitlabProjectUri?: string;  // inferred from git remote if omitted\n  envPath?: string;           // defaults to projectRoot/.env\n  runtimeOverride?: 'claude' | 'codex';\n  modelOverride?: string;\n  codexEffortOverride?: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh';\n  dryRun?: boolean;\n}\n\nexport type StepEventKind =\n  | 'start'           // step beginning\n  | 'scanning'        // querying GitLab for issues\n  | 'matched'         // found actionable issue + rule\n  | 'agent_running'   // agent dispatched, waiting\n  | 'agent_complete'  // agent finished (success or failure)\n  | 'transition'      // label transition applied\n  | 'done'            // step finished\n  | 'error';          // unrecoverable error\n\nexport interface StepEvent {\n  kind: StepEventKind;\n  ts: string;\n  data: Record<string, unknown>;  // kind-specific payload\n}\n\n/**\n * Run one factory step. Yields StepEvents during execution.\n * Final yield is always 'done' or 'error' with full StepSummary in data.\n */\nexport async function* runStep(config: StepConfig): AsyncGenerator<StepEvent, void, undefined> {\n  // ... refactored from main()\n}\n```\n\n**Existing CLI wraps the engine** — `src/runner/index.ts` becomes a thin wrapper that calls `runStep()`, collects events, and exits with the appropriate code. Zero behavior change for standalone usage.\n\n**Files to change:**\n\n| File | Change |\n|------|--------|\n| `src/runner/engine.ts` | New — extracted step logic + async generator |\n| `src/runner/index.ts` | Thin CLI wrapper calling `runStep()` |\n| `src/runner/types.ts` | Extract shared types (`StepSummary`, `StepReason`, `StepConfig`, `StepEvent`) |\n\n### 2.2 Worktree Support for Code Stages\n\nWhen the runner picks an issue that modifies code (`feat:implement`, `bug:fix`), it must isolate changes in a worktree:\n\n```\nrepo/\n├── .worktrees/\n│   ├── feat-42/     ← git worktree for feature issue #42\n│   └── bug-17/      ← git worktree for bug issue #17\n├── src/\n├── .env              ← gitignored, NOT in worktrees\n├── droidfactory.config.json  ← tracked, present in worktrees\n└── prompts/           ← tracked, present in worktrees\n```\n\n**Worktree lifecycle:**\n\n| Pipeline Event | Worktree Action |\n|---------------|----------------|\n| `feat:implement` matched | `git worktree add .worktrees/feat-<iid> -b factory/feat-<iid>` |\n| `feat:implement` agent completes | Squash-merge worktree → main, push, prune |\n| `bug:fix` matched | `git worktree add .worktrees/bug-<iid> -b factory/bug-<iid>` |\n| `bug:fix` agent completes | Squash-merge worktree → main, push, prune |\n| Agent fails | Keep worktree for retry on next loop iteration |\n\n**.env availability study:**\n\n| File | Gitignored? | In worktree? | Solution |\n|------|-------------|-------------|----------|\n| `.env` | Yes | No | Pass `--env-path` pointing to main checkout |\n| `droidfactory.config.json` | No | Yes | Available naturally |\n| `prompts/` | No | Yes | Available naturally |\n\n**Solution:** Pass explicit `--env-path` to agent runner. Docker mount: `-v ${mainCheckout}/.env:/workspace/.env:ro` regardless of worktree cwd.\n\n**Files to change:**\n\n| File | Change |\n|------|--------|\n| `src/agent-runner/index.ts` | Accept `--env-path` CLI arg |\n| `src/agent-runner/helpers/gitlab.ts` | `getGitlabEnvPath()` accepts override param |\n| `src/dispatcher/dispatch-agent.ts` | Pass `envPath` through to subprocess args |\n| `src/dispatcher/agent-dispatcher.ts` | Create/cleanup worktrees around implement/fix stages |\n| `src/agent-runner/docker/claude.ts` | Use `envPath` for `--env-file` (currently uses `options.gitlabEnvPath`, line 29) |\n| `src/agent-runner/docker/codex.ts` | Use `envPath` for `--env-file` (currently uses `.env` from cwd, line 26) |\n\n### 2.3 Per-Stage Runtime Config\n\nEvery stage uses GPT 5.3 Codex. Reasoning effort varies by complexity:\n\n| Category | Stages | Effort |\n|----------|--------|--------|\n| MACRO (analysis/planning) | analyze, plan, precheck, audit, archive, triage | `medium` |\n| MICRO (code generation) | implement, fix | `high` |\n\nConfig lives in `droidfactory.config.json` (extends existing `exec` block):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"exec\": {\n    \"defaults\": { \"runtime\": \"codex\", \"model\": \"gpt-5.3\" },\n    \"personas\": {\n      \"feature/analyzer\":    { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"feature/planner\":     { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"feature/prechecker\":  { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"feature/implementer\": { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"high\" } },\n      \"feature/auditor\":     { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"feature/archivist\":   { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"bug/triager\":         { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"bug/prechecker\":      { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"bug/fixer\":           { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"high\" } },\n      \"bug/auditor\":         { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } },\n      \"bug/archivist\":       { \"codex\": { \"reasoningEffort\": \"medium\" } }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n### 2.4 Package Export\n\nTwo integration strategies (choose one):\n\n| Strategy | Mechanism | Pros | Cons |\n|----------|-----------|------|------|\n| **Subprocess (P1)** | DroidMaster spawns `node dist/runner/index.js --json` | Zero coupling, crash isolation | Slower, parsing overhead |\n| **Library import (P2)** | `import { runStep } from 'droidfactory/engine'` | Direct event streaming, lower latency | Tighter coupling, shared process |\n\nStart with subprocess (P1). DroidFleet Factory exists at `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory`.\n+2. **Factory sources inspected.** The corrected inventory uses `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/DROIDFACTORY-OVERVIEW.md`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/droidfactory.config.json`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/src/dispatch/rules-data-pipeline-core.ts`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/src/dispatch/rules-data-pipeline-extended.ts`, and Factory role prompts under `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/prompts/`.\n+3. **Repo-local skills inspected.** DroidFleet has repo-local OpenSpec skills under `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/.codex/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`, including `openspec-new-change`, `openspec-ff-change`, `openspec-continue-change`, `openspec-explore`, `openspec-apply-change`, and `openspec-verify-change`.\n+4. **Executor skill sources inspected.** The executor family also exists under `/home/jbb/dev/AgentSkills/`, `/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.skills/`, and `/home/jbb/.codex/skills/`.\n+\n+---\n+\n+## B. OpenSpec Planning Skills In DroidFleet\n+\n+1. **`openspec-explore`.** Thinking and investigation mode. It reads code, compares options, surfaces risks, and can capture decisions into OpenSpec artifacts, but it does not implement.\n+2. **`openspec-new-change`.** Starts a new change from a goal or change name. It creates `openspec/changes/<name>/`, shows artifact status, and displays the first artifact instructions. It does not create all artifacts by itself.\n+3. **`openspec-continue-change`.** Progresses one artifact at a time. In the spec-driven schema, the sequence is `proposal.md -> specs/<capability>/spec.md -> design.md -> tasks.md`, and `tasks.md` is the checkboxed implementation task list.\n+4. **`openspec-ff-change`.** Fast-forwards artifact creation until implementation is ready. This is the strongest OpenSpec `goal -> task list` skill because it creates all required artifacts in dependency order, including `tasks.md`.\n+5. **`openspec-apply-change`.** Executes the tasks from an OpenSpec change. It is implementation, not planning, but it consumes the task list generated by the planning skills.\n+6. **`openspec-verify-change`.** Verifies implementation against `tasks`, `specs`, and `design`. It is planning-adjacent quality control, not a splitter.\n+\n+---\n+\n+## C. DroidFactory Planning Roles\n+\n+1. **`ticket/improver`.** Normalizes an existing weak issue into a factory-ready ticket. Required body structure: `Problem Report`, `REQ-###`, `Scope`, `Codebase Impact Intent`, `Dependency Blockers`, `Ideal Control-flow DAG`, and `Acceptance`. It classifies the issue as `feature` or `bug`; the orchestrator then applies `pipeline:feature + feat:plan` or `pipeline:bug + bug:rca`.\n+2. **`product/analyzer`.** Turns a vague product request into a production-grade problem definition with problem statement, goals, non-goals, scope boundaries, key unknowns, and operator-dependent integrations.\n+3. **`product/rfc-writer`.** Produces the implementation path: proposed solution, alternatives, tradeoffs, integration strategy, and mock/live switches for operator-dependent integrations.\n+4. **`product/architect`.** Defines major components, boundaries, contracts, integration switches, failure handling, observability, and rollout assumptions.\n+5. **`product/prd-writer`.** Converts approved product architecture into functional requirements, non-functional requirements, acceptance criteria, operator enablement, and release quality expectations.\n+6. **`product/decomposer`.** Splits an approved product ticket into multiple child epic tickets labeled `pipeline:epic`, `epic:research`, and `status:todo`. Each child epic includes scope, dependency/order notes, repo-grounded implementation intent, and operator integration responsibilities.\n+7. **`epic/analyzer`.** Converts an epic body into a build contract: hard specs, intent interpretation, existing data model and constraints, downstream execution contract, and proven gaps.\n+8. **`epic/architect`.** Produces the implementation plan for an epic: data model deltas, module decomposition, helper extraction plan, integration points, dependency injection boundaries, test strategy, and ordered implementation phases.\n+9. **`epic/quality-planner`.** Red-teams `Epic Architecture`, reduces over-engineering, corrects factorization, and defines non-negotiable quality gates before decomposition.\n+10. **`epic/decomposer`.** Splits corrected epic architecture into child feature issues. Each child issue is labeled `pipeline:feature`, `feat:plan`, and `status:todo`, and contains problem statement, `REQ-*`, scope, codebase impact, dependency metadata, and acceptance criteria. The parent gets an `## Epic Decomposition` note with created children, DAG summary, and readiness confirmation.\n+11. **`feature/analyzer`.** Maps feature issue intent to codebase surface area and produces an evidence-backed task breakdown, risks, planner TODOs, planner decisions, and recommended implementation order.\n+12. **`feature/planner`.** Produces the implementation plan for one feature issue: `Spec`, `Codebase Impact Intent`, `Dependency Blockers`, and `Ideal Control-flow DAG`. It does not create child issues.\n+13. **`bug/rca`.** Produces the pre-fix bug plan: reproduction status, code-path trace, root cause, fix scope, mandatory fix DAG, spec-change check, factorization check, regression test plan, and fixer checklist.\n+14. **`refactor/analyzer`.** Ranks top refactor candidates and selects the primary set for the run. It is a planning role for refactor work, but it does not create issues.\n+15. **`prototype/delivery-planner`.** Converts a design package into a delivery plan with milestones, backlog decomposition, dependency map, risk register, and validation gates.\n+\n+---\n+\n+## D. DroidFactory Pipeline Labels\n+\n+1. **Feature pipeline.** `pipeline:feature` stages include `feat:plan`, `feat:implement`, `feat:audit`, plus recovery stages such as `feat:commit_fix`, `feat:test_fix`, and `feat:merge_solve`. The first actionable feature planning stage is `feature/planner`.\n+2. **Bug pipeline.** `pipeline:bug` starts with `bug:rca`, then `bug:fix`, `bug:audit`, and `bug:archive`, with similar recovery stages. The planning stage is `bug/rca`.\n+3. **Product pipeline.** `pipeline:product` includes `analysis`, `research`, `rfc`, `architecture`, `prd`, red-team stages, and `decompose`. The final decomposition stage creates child epics.\n+4. **Epic pipeline.** `pipeline:epic` includes `research`, `analyze`, `architecture`, `quality`, `decompose`, and `review`. The decomposition stage creates child feature tickets.\n+5. **Research pipeline.** `pipeline:research` includes `scan`, `summarize`, `deep_dive`, and `conclude`. It is evidence-building rather than implementation task splitting.\n+6. **Refactor pipeline.** `pipeline:refactor` includes `analyze`, `implement`, and `audit`. The analyzer selects concrete code hygiene targets.\n+\n+---\n+\n+## E. Executor Planning Skills\n+\n+1. **`executor-precheck`.** Checks whether the operator goal has enough approved `Specs`, `Data Model`, `Runtime State`, repo facts, and scope boundary before stack planning can safely begin.\n+2. **`executor-stack`.** Analyzes specs/data/runtime, identifies `Root Blocks`, validates stack choices, creates an agnostic directory scaffold, and asks blocking operator questions.\n+3. **`executor-spec`.** Builds the `Master Ledger`: domains, one test suite per spec, inputs, effects, helpers, screens/pages, components, state, control-flow entries, unresolved questions, and spec candidates. This is the strongest executor-side `goal -> implementation structure` splitter.\n+4. **`executor-implement`.** Consumes the `Master Ledger` and implements the scaffold. It should not invent architecture or split a broad goal by itself.\n+\n+---\n+\n+## F. Extracted Decision Information\n+\n+1. **Best OpenSpec goal-to-task skill.** Use `openspec-ff-change` when the desired output is a complete OpenSpec artifact set ending in `tasks.md`.\n+2. **Best Factory issue normalizer.** Use `ticket/improver` when a rough GitLab issue must become factory-actionable with `REQ-*`, DAG, blockers, and acceptance criteria.\n+3. **Best Factory product-to-work splitter.** Use `product/decomposer` to split an approved product ticket into epics, then `epic/decomposer` to split corrected epic architecture into feature tickets.\n+4. **Best single-feature planner.** Use `feature/analyzer` before `feature/planner` when a feature needs grounded codebase surface mapping before the implementation DAG.\n+5. **Best bug planner.** Use `bug/rca`, because it produces fix scope, fix DAG, regression test plan, and fixer checklist before implementation.\n+6. **Executor vs Factory distinction.** Executor skills build a local master-ledger implementation scaffold. DroidFactory skills operate through GitLab issues and labels as the state machine.\n+7. **Correct high-level chain.** For a broad goal in DroidFactory: `ticket/improver -> product/analyzer/RFC/architecture/PRD -> product/decomposer -> epic/analyzer/architect/quality-planner -> epic/decomposer -> feature/analyzer -> feature/planner -> feature/implementer`.\n*** End Patch\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3da1-f52c-7c52-a8bd-de5a1efc1d7f"}}}

The parent gets an `## Epic Decomposition` note with created children, DAG summary, and readiness confirmation.\n11. **`feature/analyzer`.** Maps feature issue intent to codebase surface area and produces an evidence-backed task breakdown, risks, planner TODOs, planner decisions, and recommended implementation order.\n12. **`feature/planner`.** Produces the implementation plan for one feature issue: `Spec`, `Codebase Impact Intent`, `Dependency Blockers`, and `Ideal Control-flow DAG`. It does not create child issues.\n13. **`bug/rca`.** Produces the pre-fix bug plan: reproduction status, code-path trace, root cause, fix scope, mandatory fix DAG, spec-change check, factorization check, regression test plan, and fixer checklist.\n14. **`refactor/analyzer`.** Ranks top refactor candidates and selects the primary set for the run. It is a planning role for refactor work, but it does not create issues.\n15. **`prototype/delivery-planner`.** Converts a design package into a delivery plan with milestones, backlog decomposition, dependency map, risk register, and validation gates.\n\n---\n\n## D. DroidFactory Pipeline Labels\n\n1. **Feature pipeline.** `pipeline:feature` stages include `feat:plan`, `feat:implement`, `feat:audit`, plus recovery stages such as `feat:commit_fix`, `feat:test_fix`, and `feat:merge_solve`. The first actionable feature planning stage is `feature/planner`.\n2. **Bug pipeline.** `pipeline:bug` starts with `bug:rca`, then `bug:fix`, `bug:audit`, and `bug:archive`, with similar recovery stages. The planning stage is `bug/rca`.\n3. **Product pipeline.** `pipeline:product` includes `analysis`, `research`, `rfc`, `architecture`, `prd`, red-team stages, and `decompose`. The final decomposition stage creates child epics.\n4. **Epic pipeline.** `pipeline:epic` includes `research`, `analyze`, `architecture`, `quality`, `decompose`, and `review`. The decomposition stage creates child feature tickets.\n5. **Research pipeline.** `pipeline:research` includes `scan`, `summarize`, `deep_dive`, and `conclude`. It is evidence-building rather than implementation task splitting.\n6. **Refactor pipeline.** `pipeline:refactor` includes `analyze`, `implement`, and `audit`. The analyzer selects concrete code hygiene targets.\n\n---\n\n## E. Executor Planning Skills\n\n1. **`executor-precheck`.** Checks whether the operator goal has enough approved `Specs`, `Data Model`, `Runtime State`, repo facts, and scope boundary before stack planning can safely begin.\n2. **`executor-stack`.** Analyzes specs/data/runtime, identifies `Root Blocks`, validates stack choices, creates an agnostic directory scaffold, and asks blocking operator questions.\n3. **`executor-spec`.** Builds the `Master Ledger`: domains, one test suite per spec, inputs, effects, helpers, screens/pages, components, state, control-flow entries, unresolved questions, and spec candidates. This is the strongest executor-side `goal -> implementation structure` splitter.\n4. **`executor-implement`.** Consumes the `Master Ledger` and implements the scaffold. It should not invent architecture or split a broad goal by itself.\n\n---\n\n## F. Extracted Decision Information\n\n1. **Best OpenSpec goal-to-task skill.** Use `openspec-ff-change` when the desired output is a complete OpenSpec artifact set ending in `tasks.md`.\n2. **Best Factory issue normalizer.** Use `ticket/improver` when a rough GitLab issue must become factory-actionable with `REQ-*`, DAG, blockers, and acceptance criteria.\n3. **Best Factory product-to-work splitter.** Use `product/decomposer` to split an approved product ticket into epics, then `epic/decomposer` to split corrected epic architecture into feature tickets.\n4. **Best single-feature planner.** Use `feature/analyzer` before `feature/planner` when a feature needs grounded codebase surface mapping before the implementation DAG.\n5. **Best bug planner.** Use `bug/rca`, because it produces fix scope, fix DAG, regression test plan, and fixer checklist before implementation.\n6. **Executor vs Factory distinction.** Executor skills build a local master-ledger implementation scaffold. DroidFactory skills operate through GitLab issues and labels as the state machine.\n7. **Correct high-level chain.** For a broad goal in DroidFactory: `ticket/improver -> product/analyzer/RFC/architecture/PRD -> product/decomposer -> epic/analyzer/architect/quality-planner -> epic/decomposer -> feature/analyzer -> feature/planner -> feature/implementer`.\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3da1-f52c-7c52-a8bd-de5a1efc1d7f"}}}

This is the strongest executor-side `goal -> implementation structure` splitter.\n4. **`executor-implement`.** Consumes the `Master Ledger` and implements the scaffold. It should not invent architecture or split a broad goal by itself.\n\n---\n\n## F. Extracted Decision Information\n\n1. **Best OpenSpec goal-to-task skill.** Use `openspec-ff-change` when the desired output is a complete OpenSpec artifact set ending in `tasks.md`.\n2. **Best Factory issue normalizer.** Use `ticket/improver` when a rough GitLab issue must become factory-actionable with `REQ-*`, DAG, blockers, and acceptance criteria.\n3. **Best Factory product-to-work splitter.** Use `product/decomposer` to split an approved product ticket into epics, then `epic/decomposer` to split corrected epic architecture into feature tickets.\n4. **Best single-feature planner.** Use `feature/analyzer` before `feature/planner` when a feature needs grounded codebase surface mapping before the implementation DAG.\n5. **Best bug planner.** Use `bug/rca`, because it produces fix scope, fix DAG, regression test plan, and fixer checklist before implementation.\n6. **Executor vs Factory distinction.** Executor skills build a local master-ledger implementation scaffold. DroidFactory skills operate through GitLab issues and labels as the state machine.\n7. **Correct high-level chain.** For a broad goal in DroidFactory: `ticket/improver -> product/analyzer/RFC/architecture/PRD -> product/decomposer -> epic/analyzer/architect/quality-planner -> epic/decomposer -> feature/analyzer -> feature/planner -> feature/implementer`.\n","internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough":{"turn_id":"019f3dbe-c82f-7360-908f-eec78e62043f"}}}

Corrected Evidence Boundary\n\n1. **Correction.** The prior inventory was incomplete because it only searched `/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP` and missed DroidFleet. DroidFleet Factory exists at `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory`.\n2. **Factory sources inspected.** The corrected inventory uses `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/DROIDFACTORY-OVERVIEW.md`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/droidfactory.config.json`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/src/dispatch/rules-data-pipeline-core.ts`, `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/src/dispatch/rules-data-pipeline-extended.ts`, and Factory role prompts under `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/factory/prompts/`.\n3. **Repo-local skills inspected.** DroidFleet has repo-local OpenSpec skills under `/home/jbb/dev/DroidFleet/.codex/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`, including `openspec-new-change`, `openspec-ff-change`, `openspec-continue-change`, `openspec-explore`, `openspec-apply-change`, and `openspec-verify-change`.\n4. **Executor skill sources inspected.** The executor family also exists under `/home/jbb/dev/AgentSkills/`, `/home/jbb/dev/EditorBP/decision-os/.skills/`, and `/home/jbb/.codex/skills/`.\n\n---\n\n## B. OpenSpec Planning Skills In DroidFleet\n\n1. **`openspec-explore`.** Thinking and investigation mode. It reads code, compares options, surfaces risks, and can capture decisions into OpenSpec artifacts, but it does not implement.\n2. **`openspec-new-change`.** Starts a new change from a goal or change name. It creates `openspec/changes/<name>/`, shows artifact status, and displays the first artifact instructions. It does not create all artifacts by itself.\n3. **`openspec-continue-change`.** Progresses one artifact at a time. In the spec-driven schema, the sequence is `proposal.md -> specs/<capability>/spec.md -> design.md -> tasks.md`, and `tasks.md` is the checkboxed implementation task list.\n4. **`openspec-ff-change`.** Fast-forwards artifact creation until implementation is ready. This is the strongest OpenSpec `goal -> task list` skill because it creates all required artifacts in dependency order, including `tasks.md`.\n5. **`openspec-apply-change`.** Executes the tasks from an OpenSpec change. It is implementation, not planning, but it consumes the task list generated by the planning skills.\n6. **`openspec-verify-change`.** Verifies implementation against `tasks`, `specs`, and `design`. It is planning-adjacent quality control, not a splitter.\n\n---\n\n## C. DroidFactory Planning Roles\n\n1. **`ticket/improver`.** Normalizes an existing weak issue into a factory-ready ticket. Required body structure: `Problem Report`, `REQ-###`, `Scope`, `Codebase Impact Intent`, `Dependency Blockers`, `Ideal Control-flow DAG`, and `Acceptance`. It classifies the issue as `feature` or `bug`; the orchestrator then applies `pipeline:feature + feat:plan` or `pipeline:bug + bug:rca`.\n2. **`product/analyzer`.** Turns a vague product request into a production-grade problem definition with problem statement, goals, non-goals, scope boundaries, key unknowns, and operator-dependent integrations.\n3. **`product/rfc-writer`.** Produces the implementation path: proposed solution, alternatives, tradeoffs, integration strategy, and mock/live switches for operator-dependent integrations.\n4. **`product/architect`.** Defines major components, boundaries, contracts, integration switches, failure handling, observability, and rollout assumptions.\n5. **`product/prd-writer`.** Converts approved product architecture into functional requirements, non-functional requirements, acceptance criteria, operator enablement, and release quality expectations.\n6. **`product/decomposer`.** Splits an approved product ticket into multiple child epic tickets labeled `pipeline:epic`, `epic:research`, and `status:todo`. Each child epic includes scope, dependency/order notes, repo-grounded implementation intent, and operator integration responsibilities.\n7. **`epic/analyzer`.** Converts an epic body into a build contract: hard specs, intent interpretation, existing data model and constraints, downstream execution contract, and proven gaps.\n8. **`epic/architect`.** Produces the implementation plan for an epic: data model deltas, module decomposition, helper extraction plan, integration points, dependency injection boundaries, test strategy, and ordered implementation phases.\n9. **`epic/quality-planner`.** Red-teams `Epic Architecture`, reduces over-engineering, corrects factorization, and defines non-negotiable quality gates before decomposition.\n10. **`epic/decomposer`.** Splits corrected epic architecture into child feature issues. Each child issue is labeled `pipeline:feature`, `feat:plan`, and `status:todo`, and contains problem statement, `REQ-*`, scope, codebase impact, dependency metadata, and acceptance criteria. The parent gets an `## Epic Decomposition` note with created children, DAG summary, and readiness confirmation.\n11. **`feature/analyzer`.** Maps feature issue intent to codebase surface area and produces an evidence-backed task breakdown, risks, planner TODOs, planner decisions, and recommended implementation order.\n12. **`feature/planner`.** Produces the implementation plan for one feature issue: `Spec`, `Codebase Impact Intent`, `Dependency Blockers`, and `Ideal Control-flow DAG`. It does not create child issues.\n13. **`bug/rca`.** Produces the pre-fix bug plan: reproduction status, code-path trace, root cause, fix scope, mandatory fix DAG, spec-change check, factorization check, regression test plan, and fixer checklist.\n14. **`refactor/analyzer`.** Ranks top refactor candidates and selects the primary set for the run. It is a planning role for refactor work, but it does not create issues.\n15. **`prototype/delivery-planner`.** Converts a design package into a delivery plan with milestones, backlog decomposition, dependency map, risk register, and validation gates.\n\n---\n\n## D. DroidFactory Pipeline Labels\n\n1. **Feature pipeline.** `pipeline:feature` stages include `feat:plan`, `feat:implement`, `feat:audit`, plus recovery stages such as `feat:commit_fix`, `feat:test_fix`, and `feat:merge_solve`. The first actionable feature planning stage is `feature/planner`.\n2. **Bug pipeline.** `pipeline:bug` starts with `bug:rca`, then `bug:fix`, `bug:audit`, and `bug:archive`, with similar recovery stages. The planning stage is `bug/rca`.\n3. **Product pipeline.** `pipeline:product` includes `analysis`, `research`, `rfc`, `architecture`, `prd`, red-team stages, and `decompose`. The final decomposition stage creates child epics.\n4. **Epic pipeline.** `pipeline:epic` includes `research`, `analyze`, `architecture`, `quality`, `decompose`, and `review`. The decomposition stage creates child feature tickets.\n5. **Research pipeline.** `pipeline:research` includes `scan`, `summarize`, `deep_dive`, and `conclude`. It is evidence-building rather than implementation task splitting.\n6. **Refactor pipeline.** `pipeline:refactor` includes `analyze`, `implement`, and `audit`. The analyzer selects concrete code hygiene targets.\n\n---\n\n## E. Executor Planning Skills\n\n1. **`executor-precheck`.** Checks whether the operator goal has enough approved `Specs`, `Data Model`, `Runtime State`, repo facts, and scope boundary before stack planning can safely begin.\n2. **`executor-stack`.** Analyzes specs/data/runtime, identifies `Root Blocks`, validates stack choices, creates an agnostic directory scaffold, and asks blocking operator questions.\n3. **`executor-spec`.** Builds the `Master Ledger`: domains, one test suite per spec, inputs, effects, helpers, screens/pages, components, state, control-flow entries, unresolved questions, and spec candidates. This is the strongest executor-side `goal -> implementation structure` splitter.\n4. **`executor-implement`.** Consumes the `Master Ledger` and implements the scaffold. It should not invent architecture or split a broad goal by itself.\n\n---\n\n## F. Extracted Decision Information\n\n1. **Best OpenSpec goal-to-task skill.** Use `openspec-ff-change` when the desired output is a complete OpenSpec artifact set ending in `tasks.md`.\n2. **Best Factory issue normalizer.** Use `ticket/improver` when a rough GitLab issue must become factory-actionable with `REQ-*`, DAG, blockers, and acceptance criteria.\n3. **Best Factory product-to-work splitter.** Use `product/decomposer` to split an approved product ticket into epics, then `epic/decomposer` to split corrected epic architecture into feature tickets.\n4. **Best single-feature planner.** Use `feature/analyzer` before `feature/planner` when a feature needs grounded codebase surface mapping before the implementation DAG.\n5. **Best bug planner.** Use `bug/rca`, because it produces fix scope, fix DAG, regression test plan, and fixer checklist before implementation.\n6. **Executor vs Factory distinction.** Executor skills build a local master-ledger implementation scaffold. DroidFactory skills operate through GitLab issues and labels as the state machine.\n7. **Correct high-level chain.** For a broad goal in DroidFactory: `ticket/improver -> product/analyzer/RFC/architecture/PRD -> product/decomposer -> epic/analyzer/architect/quality-planner -> epic/decomposer -> feature/analyzer -> feature/planner -> feature/implementer`.\n"}},"status":"completed"}}

When asked to show the output of a command (e.g. `git show`), relay the important details in your answer or summarize the key lines so the user understands the result.\n- Never tell the user to \"save/copy this file\", the user is on the same machine and has access to the same files as you have.\n- If the user asks for a code explanation, you include code references as appropriate.\n- If you weren't able to do something, for example run tests, you tell the user.\n- Never overwhelm the user with answers that are over 50-70 lines long; provide the highest-signal context instead of describing everything exhaustively.\n- Tone of your final answer must match your personality.\n- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.\n\n## Intermediary updates\n\n- Intermediary updates go to the `commentary` channel.\n- User updates are short updates while you are working, they are NOT final answers.\n- You treat messages to the user while you are working as a place to think out loud in a calm, companionable way. You casually explain what you are doing and why in one or two sentences.\n- Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like \"I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>\", \"I will do <X>, not <Y>\".\n- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.\n- You provide user updates frequently, every 30s.\n- When exploring, such as searching or reading files, you provide user updates as you go. You explain what context you are gathering and what you are learning. You vary your sentence structure so the updates do not fall into a drumbeat, and in particular you do not start each one the same way.\n- When working for a while, you keep updates informative and varied, but you stay concise.\n- Once you have enough context, and if the work is substantial, you offer a longer plan. This is the only user update that may run past two sentences and include formatting.\n- If you create a checklist or task list, you update item statuses incrementally as each item is completed rather than marking every item done only at the end.\n- Before performing file edits of any kind, you provide updates explaining what edits you are making.\n- Tone of your updates must match your personality.\n"},"git":{"commit_hash":"9d6b43c46c474d1919b3730e195e3fd438131445","branch":"master","repository_url":"git@github.com:MohLePatron/moh-root-repo.git"}}}

sleep 1\"},\n    43\t\t\t\t\tCache:   CacheConfig{Mode: \"read_seed_only\", SeedRoot: \".cache/fail\", RunRoot: \".cache/run-fail/{run_id}\"},\n    44\t\t\t\t},\n    45\t\t\t\t\"slow\": {\n    46\t\t\t\t\tWorkdir: \".\",\n    47\t\t\t\t\tCommand: []string{\"bash\", \"-lc\", \"sleep 30\"},\n    48\t\t\t\t\tCache:   CacheConfig{Mode: \"read_seed_only\", SeedRoot: \".cache/slow\", RunRoot: \".cache/run-slow/{run_id}\"},\n    49\t\t\t\t},\n    50\t\t\t},\n    51\t\t}\n    52\t\n    53\t\tbegin := time.Now()\n    54\t\tengine.executeRun(runCtx, spec, map[string]Domain{\"fail\": spec.Domains[\"fail\"], \"slow\": spec.Domains[\"slow\"]}, []string{\"fail\", \"slow\"}, handle)\n    55\t\telapsed := time.Since(begin)\n    56\t\tif elapsed > 10*time.Second {\n    57\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected global fail-fast cancellation under 10s, got %v\", elapsed)\n    58\t\t}\n    59\t\n    60\t\tstatus := cloneStatus(handle.status)\n    61\t\tif status.Status != \"failed\" {\n    62\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected overall status failed, got %q\", status.Status)\n    63\t\t}\n    64\t\tif status.Domains[\"fail\"].Status != \"failed\" {\n    65\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected fail domain status failed, got %q\", status.Domains[\"fail\"].Status)\n    66\t\t}\n    67\t\tif status.Domains[\"slow\"].Status != \"failed\" {\n    68\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected slow domain canceled-by-fail status failed, got %q\", status.Domains[\"slow\"].Status)\n    69\t\t}\n    70\t\tif !strings.Contains(status.Domains[\"fail\"].Error, \"fail-fast\") {\n    71\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected fail domain error to include fail-fast, got %q\", status.Domains[\"fail\"].Error)\n    72\t\t}\n    73\t\tif !strings.Contains(status.Domains[\"slow\"].Error, \"context canceled\") {\n    74\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected slow domain cancellation error, got %q\", status.Domains[\"slow\"].Error)\n    75\t\t}\n    76\t}\n"}}

Finalize with a clean worktree:\n   - Run `git status --porcelain` in the active worktree.\n   - End only with empty output.\n   - Commit intended conflict-resolution changes before finishing.\n   - Remove accidental/untracked artifacts not meant for delivery.\n\nRules:\n- Avoid blind conflict resolution.\n- Preserve correctness of the original bug fix first.\n- Escalate unresolved semantic ambiguity in the report.\n- Do not leave unrelated issue commits in the branch history.\n- Never finish with uncommitted changes in the worktree.\n- Do NOT call `mcp__gitlab-mcp__create_issue_note` or post any GitLab note/comment.\n\n\nUSER PROMPT:\n## Issue IID\n278\n\n## Issue Title\nMCP UI: keep action buttons pinned, enable internal card scroll, and keep message input always visible\n\n## Original Issue Content\n## Problem\nLong `ui.roadmap` / `ui.plan_block` / proposal cards can occupy the full viewport and trap interaction.\n\nObserved failures:\n- Action buttons (approve/reject/confirm) are not reliably reachable when card content is very long.\n- Card content cannot always be scrolled internally, causing a deadlock state.\n- Composer area (text + voice message input) becomes hidden/blocked by the MCP UI card layer.\n- User cannot reject/confirm and cannot send a new message in some states.\n\n## Required behavior\n1. MCP UI cards must keep action buttons pinned at the bottom of the card view.\n2. Card body/content must be independently scrollable inside the card.\n3. The main message composer (text + voice) must stay visible and usable at all times.\n4. No MCP UI card should be able to fully block conversation input.\n\n## Scope\n- All MCP UI card types with actions (`ui.roadmap`, `ui.plan_block`, `ui.tasks`, suggestion/approval cards).\n- Mobile and desktop layouts.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n1. For long card payloads, user can scroll card content and still reach action buttons.\n2. Action bar remains anchored to the bottom of the card/container while content scrolls.\n3. Message composer remains visible and interactive while card is displayed.\n4. User can always either:\n   - act on the card (confirm/reject), or\n   - send a text/voice message without dismiss deadlock.\n5. Regression tests (or UI interaction tests) cover long-content cards and verify no input-blocking state.\n\n## Priority\nHigh (interaction deadlock / operator blocked).\n\n## Thread (All Notes)\n### Note 1 [Note] (2026-03-27T11:33:44.730Z by @bot)\n## Pre-Fix Check\n\n### Verdict: NEEDS_ATTENTION\nCurrent tests cover basic pinned-card/input behavior, but do not cover the long-content deadlock path required by this bug.\n\n### Q1: Spec Modifications\n**Answer**: NO\n- Evidence:\n  - `app/lib/state/models/event_data_ui.dart`\n  - `app/lib/data/event_codec_decode.dart`\n  - `app/lib/data/event_codec_encode.dart`\n  - `app/lib/data/event_codec_mappers.dart`\n- Handling (if YES):\n  - N/A\n\n### Q2: Duplication / Factorization\n**Answer**: YES\n- Evidence:\n  - Action rendering is duplicated across cards:\n    - `app/lib/ui/widgets/event_cards/action_card.dart`\n    - `app/lib/ui/widgets/event_cards/plan_block_card.dart`\n    - `app/lib/ui/widgets/event_cards/tasks_card.dart`\n    - `app/lib/ui/widgets/event_cards/roadmap_card.dart`\n  - Each card currently builds its own content + action button block; implementing sticky bottom actions separately in each would duplicate layout logic.\n- Proposed factorization (if YES):\n  - Extract a shared card shell for actionable MCP cards (scrollable body + pinned action bar), then use it in Action/Plan/Tasks/Roadmap cards.\n\n### Q3: Test Coverage + Regression Test (mandatory)\n**Answer**: GAPS_FOUND\n- Existing relevant tests:\n  - `app/test/widget/screens/keyboard_shortcuts_sticky_approval_test.dart` (pinned card presence only)\n  - `app/test/widget/conversation/input_bar_test.dart` (input enabled/basic send)\n  - `app/test/widget/event_cards/plan_block_card_test.dart` (plan card rendering)\n  - `app/test/widget/event_cards/tasks_roadmap_review_cards_test.dart` (tasks/roadmap rendering)\n- Required regression test (must be specific to this bug):\n  - Setup: Build `DroidScreen` (mobile and desktop surface sizes) with a pending `planBlock`/`roadmap` action whose markdown/body is intentionally very long (enough to exceed viewport), and include active input bar (text + voice enabled flags used by screen).\n  - Trigger: Scroll inside the pinned MCP card body to near bottom, then attempt both flows: tap pinned action button and interact with composer (`enterText` + send, and voice control presence/tapability).\n  - Assert: (1) action bar remains visible/anchored while card body scrolls, (2) card body is internally scrollable, (3) composer remains visible and interactive, (4) no state where neither action buttons nor composer are reachable.\n  - Suggested location: `app/test/widget/screens/mcp_ui_card_scroll_and_composer_regression_test.dart`\n\n### Fixer Checklist (must-do)\n- [ ] Write the regression test first (it must fail pre-fix)\n- [ ] Ensure Q1 handling is respected (if YES)\n- [ ] Avoid adding duplication; apply factorization if required (if YES)\n- [ ] Run full test suite after the fix\n\n### Summary\nPrimary risk is fixing one card type or one breakpoint while leaving other actionable cards/mobile layout in deadlock-prone states. Ready to fix means a shared layout path is used and regression tests prove action reachability plus composer availability under long-content conditions.\n\n### Note 2 [Note] (2026-03-27T11:45:05.783Z by @bot)\n## Fix Report\n\n### Root Cause Confirmation\n- Triaged root cause: confirmed\n- Notes: Long actionable cards were rendered with unconstrained natural height in pinned column position, so long markdown expanded the card, pushed interactive controls off-screen, and caused RenderFlex overflow/deadlock states.\n\n### What Was Fixed\n- Added a shared actionable-card shell that constrains card height, provides internal body scrolling, and keeps the action area pinned at the bottom.\n- Migrated `ActionCard`, `PlanBlockCard`, `TasksCard`, and `RoadmapCard` to the shared shell to remove
